\chapter{A Sentence Inside a Sentence}
\label{ch:mr-clause-inside-clause}
\hlchaptermodality{35}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can report what I think or know with a whole clause after ki, and turn any Marathi verb into a purpose with -nyaasaathii.}

Complete MR-R35-inside and produce a reason, a reported thought and an aim, naming what each underneath clause is doing.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kī]{\mr{की} (kī) — that}

\label{lesson:MR-C35-kii}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the two items before this one by name: \textbf{\mr{कारण}}, which puts a reason under a claim, and the comma that carries a written list. Then say \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{वाटतं}} — \emph{it seems to me}. You have had the verb for a long time and have never once been able to say WHAT seems.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \mr{की} opens the room where the thought goes}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{वाटतं} \mr{की} \mr{चहा} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{malā vāṭtaṁ kī chahā āhe.} — \textbf{I think there is tea.}
\end{quote}

Word for word that is \emph{to-me it-seems \textbf{that} tea is}. Everything after \textbf{\mr{की}} is an ordinary complete Marathi sentence — \textbf{\mr{चहा} \mr{आहे}} — doing the job of an object.

That is the trick worth seeing: you do not need a new grammar to report a thought. You need one word and a sentence you could already say. Every sentence in this book just became something you can think, know or say \emph{about}.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{आहे} \mr{की} \mr{चहा} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{I know that there is tea.}
\end{quote}

Negate the outer half and the inner clause survives untouched: \textbf{\mr{मला} \mr{माहीत} \mr{नाही} \mr{की} \mr{चहा} \mr{आहे}} — \emph{I don't know whether there is tea.} Only the main verb was denied.

\textbf{\mr{कारण}} and \textbf{\mr{की}} are cousins in shape and different in job: \textbf{\mr{कारण}} puts a clause underneath as a REASON, \textbf{\mr{की}} puts one underneath as the CONTENT. Both keep the main clause first, which is Marathi's steady habit.

\textbf{\mr{की}} comes from the same Sanskrit question stem \textbf{\mr{क}-} that gave you \textbf{\mr{का}} and \textbf{\mr{काय}}. Persian does exactly the same thing with its own \emph{ke}, and for the same reason: a question word is already a placeholder, so it is the natural thing to put where a whole sentence is about to arrive.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chahā āhe} on its own
  \item \emph{malā vāṭtaṁ kī chahā āhe}
  \item what changed inside the second half when you put it after \textbf{\mr{की}} — \textbf{nothing}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What goes after \textbf{\mr{की}}? (\textbf{A whole ordinary sentence, unchanged}.) How does \textbf{\mr{की}} differ from \textbf{\mr{कारण}}? (\textbf{\mr{कारण} gives the reason; \mr{की} gives the content}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%80}{Wiktionary: \mr{की}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ṇyāsāṭhī]{-\mr{ण्यासाठी} (-ṇyāsāṭhī) — in order to}

\label{lesson:MR-C35-saathi}



\begin{quote}
Every Marathi verb in this book ends in \textbf{-\mr{णे}}: \textbf{\mr{शिकणे}}, \textbf{\mr{वाचणे}}, \textbf{\mr{बोलणे}}. That ending is what makes the verb usable as a \emph{thing}. Now it becomes usable as a \emph{purpose}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: swap -\mr{णे} for -\mr{ण्यासाठी}}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मराठी} \mr{शिकण्यासाठी} \mr{वाचतो}.} — \emph{mī marāṭhī shikṇyāsāṭhī vācto.} — \textbf{I read in order to learn Marathi.}
\end{quote}

One swap does it — take \textbf{-\mr{णे}} off, put \textbf{-\mr{ण्यासाठी}} on:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{dictionary form} & \textbf{purpose form} \\
\midrule
\mr{शिकणे} & \mr{शिकण्यासाठी} \\
\mr{वाचणे} & \mr{वाचण्यासाठी} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The purpose clause then goes BEFORE the main verb, which is where Marathi keeps everything that modifies it.

Two honest notes. First, \textbf{\mr{साठी}} is a postposition meaning \emph{for the sake of} — it can sit after a plain noun too. Second, the \textbf{-\mr{ण्या}-} in front of it is not decoration: Marathi bends a word into an \emph{oblique} shape before any postposition, and this is one instance of a rule that runs through the whole language. That general rule is still owed to you. Learn this one swap now; the rule it belongs to comes later.

Where \textbf{\mr{कारण}} answers \emph{why} by giving a cause, \textbf{-\mr{ण्यासाठी}} answers it by giving an aim. Marathi keeps those apart and you now have both.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{shikṇe} $\to$ \emph{shikṇyāsāṭhī}, then \emph{vācṇe} $\to$ \emph{vācṇyāsāṭhī}
  \item \emph{mī marāṭhī shikṇyāsāṭhī vācto}
  \item the difference between a cause and an aim — \emph{kāraṇ} against \emph{-ṇyāsāṭhī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you take off the verb, and what do you put on? (\textbf{Take off -\mr{णे}, put on -\mr{ण्यासाठी}}.) Where does the purpose clause stand? (\textbf{Before the main verb}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%A0\%E0\%A5\%80}{Wiktionary: \mr{साठी}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… kī … · -ṇyāsāṭhī …]{Three clauses underneath, three jobs}

\label{lesson:MR-R35-inside}



\begin{quote}
Three things can now go underneath a Marathi main clause: a reason, a content, and an aim. Name the word or ending that carries each.

Then reach further back and say the frame that shares a pair out — \textbf{\mr{एक}} in front of one, \textbf{\mr{दुसरा}} in front of the other — and notice that it puts its two halves side by side as equals, which is exactly what these three do not do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the \textbf{\mr{कारण}} sentence
  \item the \textbf{\mr{की}} sentence
  \item the \textbf{-\mr{ण्यासाठी}} sentence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three goes BEFORE the main verb rather than after it? (\textbf{The -\mr{ण्यासाठी} purpose clause}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
